paragraphs.text: A [Tieguanyin](tieguanyin:definition) from Anxi County in southern Fujian, made in 1970 the older way: oxidised further than most of today's tea and roasted over charcoal. Roasted tea was the norm then. The [light green style](tieguanyin:styles) only took over in Anxi from the 1990s, two decades after this leaf was made.

The heavier roast is the steadier kind, and it is the kind people keep for years, while the light style goes stale quickly. After fifty-six years the roast has long since settled, and the tea is what the trade calls [old Tie](tieguanyin:ageing), lǎo tiě: Tieguanyin that has changed with age, not just with how it was made.

brewing.text: Tieguanyin is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C; the light green style is often taken a little cooler, about 85 to 95°C. Use about 4 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 150 ml gaiwan or pot, about a third full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 10 to 30 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and a good Tieguanyin gives about six to eight. In a larger pot, use about 2.5 to 5 grams for 240 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: A smoother, rounder, softer cup with the fire gone, a liquor turned orange-red or reddish-brown, and often a soft fruity sourness.
